doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Quitting commercials and the three-martini lunch
summary: A brush-off meeting made him quit and return to playing; he learned daytime drinking.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: of the meeting they said, “Chico, we’ll call you.” Just like that. So I got up and I walked to the elevator and I punched the elevator, and as I was waiting for the elevator to come up, all of a sudden the realization just hit me, just don’t call us, we’ll call you. And man I just said screw this. And that’s it. I stopped. I came home, came back to my office, I told my wife I said, “Hey, listen Babes, I’ve had it. I’m going to start doing what I’m supposed to be doing again. I’m going to start playing again.” And I started.
All right. So how long a span of years was that?
Well I started, let’s see, from ’66 ‘till up in the ‘70s, up until the ‘80s maybe. It was long.
Wow. That’s a high pressure world to be in, isn’t it.
Oh yeah. Man I learned how to drink in the daytime. You know, the three martini lunch. I had never drank before in my life in the daytime you know? I learned that.
It’s unbelievable man. But anyway, it was good though. I made a lot of dough. But what good is the dough when you kind of lose something.
